meta.statement: This is a self-assessment. No third-party audit or certification has been performed. The register, the method and the accepted risks are published so that the assessment can be independently checked by anyone with a clone of the repository.

out_of_scope: web/ — the Vue single-page frontend, assessed separately
packages/ — the C# and TypeScript client SDKs, assessed separately
Operator deployment configuration beyond the shipped Helm chart
cmd/bridge and the honeypot profile, which are non-default deployment modes
scope.asvs_level_note: Every ASVS 5.0.0 requirement at L1 and L2 is classified. L3 requirements are outside the declared level; where one is nevertheless satisfied or deliberately not satisfied it is recorded anyway rather than omitted.

meta.claim: Every requirement in scope is classified Met, Accepted Risk, or Not Applicable. There are no unclassified requirements and no open Gap findings. Every Met requirement names at least one test in tests/compliance/ that runs on every CI build. Every Accepted Risk carries a rationale, a compensating control, a residual-risk statement, a revisit condition and a named accepting party. Every Not Applicable requirement carries the reason it does not apply.
meta.no_percentages: This register deliberately publishes no coverage percentage. A percentage requires a weighting model and a denominator; publishing the register instead lets a reader compute whatever figure they consider meaningful, and check it.

AR-13.title: Concurrent-session cap is soft, not strictly enforced
AR-13.rationale: The cap counts distinct token families and then inserts, without a lock, so simultaneous logins can overshoot it. The argument for accepting this is written in the code it describes, at internal/service/auth.go:1115-1124: the over-count is bounded by the number of racing logins, converges as families expire, and confers no authentication bypass. It is a resource control, not a security boundary.
AR-13.compensating_control: Per-user and per-IP rate limiting on the login endpoint bounds how many simultaneous logins an attacker can mount; families expire on the refresh TTL.
AR-13.residual_risk: A user may briefly hold more concurrent sessions than the configured cap.
AR-13.revisit_when: The cap becomes a hard security boundary rather than a resource control, or a customer contract specifies strict enforcement.
AR-13.cost_of_closing: A per-user advisory lock or a count-conditional INSERT on the login hot path.

AR-14.title: No inactivity timeout, and the absolute session lifetime defaults well above the AAL2 recommendation
AR-14.rationale: The mandatory half of SP 800-63B-4 section 2.2.3 is satisfied as of 1.0.0: migration 013 gives every rotation family a stored birth date that rotation cannot advance and pruning cannot reset, TokenService clamps a rotated pair to that origin plus the bound, AuthService.enforceSessionLifetime refuses a family past it and fails closed when the age cannot be determined, and cmd/vault/main.go:317 configures it from VAULT_MAX_SESSION_LIFETIME. Two advisory halves remain open. The default overall timeout is 720 hours where section 2.2.3 says it SHOULD be no more than 24 at AAL2, because a 24-hour default would force a daily re-login on a general-purpose authentication server whose deployments are not all AAL2. And there is no inactivity timeout at all: no column records last activity and no auth decision consults one.
AR-14.compensating_control: Access tokens live 15 minutes; every refresh re-checks account state, re-verifies the device fingerprint, and rotates the token single-use with family revocation on replay; the absolute family bound is enforced and fails closed; users and administrators can revoke all sessions; the per-user session cap bounds how many can exist. An operator who needs the AAL2 figure can set VAULT_MAX_SESSION_LIFETIME=24h today.
AR-14.residual_risk: A session left idle is not terminated for inactivity, and the shipped default permits a continuously-refreshing client to hold one session for 30 days.
AR-14.revisit_when: Any deployment claims AAL2 conformance to a third party rather than self-assessing, in which case the default must move to 24 hours and an inactivity timeout must ship. Also revisit if a customer contract specifies an idle policy.
AR-14.cost_of_closing: For the default: one constant, plus a documented migration note because shortening it logs every existing session out. For inactivity: a last_activity_at column on auth.refresh_tokens, a write on every refresh, and a check before rotation.

AR-15.title: Security events are logged but nothing alerts on them
AR-15.rationale: risk_score is a hardcoded per-event severity tag, not a computed score, and the code says so at internal/adminapi/handler.go:503-505. Nothing reads it for a decision: AuditFilter supports user, event type and time window only, there is no WHERE risk_score clause anywhere, and no threshold constant exists. The honeypot Alerter is the only outbound channel, it is a concrete struct with an inlined HTTP client rather than a dispatcher, and internal/server/server.go:140-141 installs it only in the honeypot profile, so in production it is never wired at all.
AR-15.compensating_control: Every security-relevant event is recorded in an append-only store with the metadata needed to investigate, and the admin gateway exposes a filtered review interface. Detection is operator-driven rather than automated.
AR-15.residual_risk: A slow credential-stuffing campaign or a data-access anomaly is visible in the audit trail but raises nothing, so time-to-detection depends on an operator looking.
AR-15.revisit_when: Before any deployment where vault42 is the controller rather than the processor, or where an Art. 33 72-hour clock could plausibly start without an operator noticing.
AR-15.cost_of_closing: A risk-score predicate on AuditFilter, a threshold constant, an extracted Dispatcher interface from the honeypot alerter, and removal of the profile gate on the risk path.

AR-16.title: RBAC permission denials on the admin plane are not audited
AR-16.rationale: internal/adminapi/middleware.go RBACCheck answers 403 insufficient_permissions and returns without writing an audit record. Failed admin authentication, lockout and the killswitch trip are all logged; only the authorization decision is not.
AR-16.compensating_control: The denial is still enforced. The admin plane is loopback-only behind mutual TLS with a verified client certificate, so the set of principals that could generate a denial is small, enumerated and already authenticated.
AR-16.residual_risk: An administrator probing beyond their role leaves no trail, so privilege-boundary probing is not detectable after the fact.
AR-16.revisit_when: The admin plane becomes reachable from anything other than loopback, or the number of administrator accounts grows past the point where they are individually known.
AR-16.cost_of_closing: One audit.Log call in RBACCheck. It needs the audit logger threaded into the middleware, which is why it was not a one-line change.

AR-17.title: No allowlist is enforced at the outbound HTTP client layer
AR-17.rationale: Every outbound destination is operator-configured rather than caller-supplied: the OIDC issuer, the SMTP relay, the HIBP range API and the honeypot webhook. There is no request path that lets a caller influence a destination, so the server-side request forgery precondition is absent. What is missing is defence in depth: no code-level allowlist would stop an operator misconfiguration from pointing the server somewhere unintended.
AR-17.compensating_control: The OIDC issuer is pinned against its own discovery document; the chart's NetworkPolicy restricts egress to Postgres, Redis, DNS and a configured SMTP CIDR, which enforces the allowlist at the network layer instead.
AR-17.residual_risk: An operator who misconfigures an issuer or webhook URL gets no code-level warning.
AR-17.revisit_when: Any feature accepts a URL from a request.
AR-17.cost_of_closing: A shared http.Client with a dial-time destination check.

AR-18.title: No notification of authentication attempts from an unusual location
AR-18.rationale: ASVS 5.0.0 V6.3.5 is an L3 requirement and vault42 is assessed at L2. It is recorded rather than omitted because the omission is deliberate: implementing it requires IP geolocation, and vault42 deliberately does not geolocate, pseudonymising addresses to a /24 or /64 before they reach any log.
AR-18.compensating_control: Lockout notifications are sent; users can list their own active sessions and devices and revoke any of them.
AR-18.residual_risk: A successful authentication with stolen valid credentials from a new location is not proactively surfaced to the user.
AR-18.revisit_when: vault42 is assessed at L3, or a deployment accepts the privacy cost of geolocation.
AR-18.cost_of_closing: A geolocation dependency and a change to the data-minimisation position in docs/PRIVACY.md, which is the reason this is not simply a feature.

AR-20.title: Authenticator loss is handled by operator escrow, not by repeated identity proofing
AR-20.rationale: ASVS 5.0.0 V6.4.4 requires evidence of identity proofing at the same level as enrollment when a factor is lost. vault42 performs no identity proofing at enrollment, so there is no level to match; the requirement presumes an identity-proofing CSP that vault42 is not.
AR-20.compensating_control: Backup codes are issued at enrollment; beyond those, recovery requires the operator-held escrow, which needs a private key held offline and outside the system.
AR-20.residual_risk: Account recovery ultimately rests on operator process rather than on a technical proof of identity.
AR-20.revisit_when: vault42 gains an identity-proofing step at enrollment.
AR-20.cost_of_closing: Not applicable without an identity-proofing capability.

AR-21.title: Tokens carry no acr, amr or aal claim
AR-21.rationale: AuthenticatorAssuranceLevel constants and AALForMethods exist at internal/service/mfa.go:16-79 and are unit-tested, but AALForMethods has no non-test caller and VaultClaims carries no acr, amr or aal field, so a resource server cannot ask which factors were used or how recently.
AR-21.compensating_control: A resource server can require a scope that vault42 only issues after MFA, which gives a coarser version of the same guarantee.
AR-21.residual_risk: A downstream service cannot distinguish a single-factor session from a multi-factor one from the token alone.
AR-21.revisit_when: A relying party needs step-up authentication, or vault42 claims AAL2 conformance to a third party rather than self-assessing it.
AR-21.cost_of_closing: Record the factor used at CompleteMFALogin, add the claim at issuance, and surface aal_level on the MFA status response. Note the trap: MFAStatus.Methods holds enrolled methods and never contains the password, so passing it to AALForMethods naively returns AAL1 for a password-plus-TOTP user.

AR-22.title: Identity provider session lifetime is not tracked
AR-22.rationale: A federated session is bound to vault42's own lifetime. vault42 does not record the IdP's auth_time or force reauthentication when the maximum interval since the IdP authentication event elapses.
AR-22.compensating_control: The vault42 session is independently bounded by its own refresh TTL, is revocable by the user and by an administrator, and re-checks account state on every rotation.
AR-22.residual_risk: A user whose IdP session was terminated upstream keeps their vault42 session until it expires or is revoked.
AR-22.revisit_when: A deployment federates to an IdP whose session policy is the authoritative one, such as a corporate SSO with mandatory reauthentication.
AR-22.cost_of_closing: Record auth_time from the ID token and compare it on refresh.

AR-23.title: Outbound SMTP negotiates STARTTLS opportunistically with no minimum version
AR-23.rationale: internal/email/smtp.go calls net/smtp.SendMail. Two behaviours have to be separated. When the relay advertises STARTTLS, SendMail negotiates it and RETURNS the error rather than continuing in the clear, so there is no silent downgrade on a failed handshake. When the relay does not advertise STARTTLS at all, the whole block is skipped and the message is sent in plaintext, and there is no setting that makes TLS mandatory. That is the exposure: an on-path attacker who strips the STARTTLS capability from the EHLO response reads the message. SendMail does pass a tls.Config (ServerName only); MinVersion is unset but Go clients default to TLS 1.2, so the negotiated version is not the weakness. The SendGrid path is HTTPS with the Go default TLS configuration.
AR-23.compensating_control: Mail carries no credential: only single-use, short-lived links and codes. The chart's NetworkPolicy restricts SMTP egress to a configured CIDR, so the relay is not an arbitrary host, and docs flag smtpCIDR as needing production restriction.
AR-23.residual_risk: Against a relay that does not offer STARTTLS, or an on-path attacker stripping the capability from EHLO, a verification link or OTP traverses the network in the clear. Credentials are not exposed when SMTP AUTH is configured: smtp.PlainAuth refuses to send over an unencrypted connection. A deployment with no SMTP AUTH has no such protection.
AR-23.revisit_when: Any credential-bearing content is added to an email, or a deployment cannot restrict SMTP egress by CIDR.
AR-23.cost_of_closing: Replace SendMail with an explicit smtp.Client, require STARTTLS unless an operator opts out, and keep the Go default MinVersion. Small change, but it alters the outbound mail path and cannot be verified here without a real MTA.

AR-24.title: The audit log is not cryptographically chained and is not mirrored off-system
AR-24.rationale: Hash chaining defends against an adversary who already holds database write access. Against that adversary a chain whose signing key lives in the same process is theatre: the adversary rewrites the rows and re-signs them. The honest version needs an off-box key and an off-system mirror, which is a deployment-topology commitment rather than a code change. Meanwhile the trigger and grant model already defeats the realistic adversary, a compromised vault_app role.
AR-24.compensating_control: audit.deny_modify() raises on UPDATE and DELETE; UPDATE and DELETE are revoked from vault_app; the one sanctioned deletion path is SECURITY DEFINER with a pinned search_path, EXECUTE revoked from PUBLIC, and the trigger re-enabled before it returns.
AR-24.residual_risk: An adversary holding database superuser access can rewrite history without leaving evidence in the log itself.
AR-24.revisit_when: 1.1, together with an off-system mirror. A chain designed without one would be worse than none because it would imply a guarantee it does not provide.
AR-24.cost_of_closing: A prev-hash column, a signing key held outside the process, read-time verification, and a checkpoint scheme that survives retention pruning. The batch insert path at internal/repository/postgres/audit.go:50 breaks a naive prev-hash chain and is the hard part.

AR-25.title: DPoP proofs are validated but no token is sender-constrained, and some decrypted buffers are not zeroed
AR-25.rationale: Two related residuals in the same area. First, DPoP: internal/crypto/dpop.go validates a proof thoroughly, but no issuance path sets cnf.jkt, so claims.Confirmation is always nil and internal/middleware/dpop.go binds nothing. The code documents itself as experimental, VAULT_DPOP_ENABLED is off by default, and the discovery document does not advertise DPoP, so nothing is claimed to clients that is not delivered. Second, memory zeroing: the master key, KMS root key and HMAC secret are []byte and are zeroed, but the decrypted RSA private signing key PEM at internal/keystore/keystore.go:297 is not, nor are decrypted blob plaintexts and labels, the identity JSON before encryption, or the user and admin TOTP secrets. Eleven configuration secrets are Go strings and cannot be zeroed at all, which is the platform limitation already accepted as AR-4.
AR-25.compensating_control: The process is short-lived and containerised with no core dumps; the signing key is regenerated on rotation; ASVS 5.0.0 removed the memory-zeroing requirement that the previous report filed this under (v4.0.3-8.3.2 is marked DELETED, NOT IN SCOPE in the official mapping), and the only surviving related requirement, V11.7.1 full memory encryption, is L3.
AR-25.residual_risk: A heap dump taken while the process is live could yield the JWT signing key or recently decrypted personal data.
AR-25.revisit_when: Either capability is advertised to a customer, or a deployment requires memory-dump resistance. Retracting the DPoP surface is preferable to leaving it half-built past 1.0.0.
AR-25.cost_of_closing: For DPoP: set cnf.jkt at issuance when a proof was presented, or remove the middleware. For zeroing: defer config.ZeroBytes on the keystore PEM and the blob and TOTP buffers, which is roughly a day and does not close the Go string half.

requirements.requirement: Verify that input is decoded or unescaped into a canonical form only once, it is only decoded when encoded data in that form is expected, and that this is done before processing the input further, for example it is not performed after input validation or sanitization.
requirements.notes: Input is decoded once by net/http and encoding/json; sanitize.String escapes on the way out, not on the way in.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application performs output encoding and escaping either as a final step before being used by the interpreter for which it is intended or by the interpreter itself.
requirements.notes: Encoding is applied at the boundary of the interpreter that consumes the value.

requirements.requirement: Verify that output encoding for an HTTP response, HTML document, or XML document is relevant for the context required, such as encoding the relevant characters for HTML elements, HTML attributes, HTML comments, CSS, or HTTP header fields, to avoid changing the message or document structure.
requirements.notes: Responses are JSON produced by encoding/json, which escapes by construction; X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops a client reinterpreting them.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when dynamically building URLs, untrusted data is encoded according to its context (e.g., URL encoding or base64url encoding for query or path parameters). Ensure that only safe URL protocols are permitted (e.g., disallow javascript: or data:).
requirements.notes: RedirectPath rejects scheme-relative and absolute targets; AvatarURL is HTTPS-only.

requirements.requirement: Verify that output encoding or escaping is used when dynamically building JavaScript content (including JSON), to avoid changing the message or document structure (to avoid JavaScript and JSON injection).
requirements.notes: All JSON is produced by encoding/json. No response is assembled by string concatenation.

requirements.requirement: Verify that data selection or database queries (e.g., SQL, HQL, NoSQL, Cypher) use parameterized queries, ORMs, entity frameworks, or are otherwise protected from SQL Injection and other database injection attacks. This is also relevant when writing stored procedures.
requirements.notes: Every query in the repository layer is parameterised. Enforced structurally over all 139 call sites, with a negative control proving the detector fires.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application protects against OS command injection and that operating system calls use parameterized OS queries or use contextual command line output encoding.
requirements.notes: vault42 makes no operating-system calls. os/exec is not imported anywhere under internal/ or cmd/.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities, or that specific security controls to prevent LDAP injection have been implemented.
requirements.notes: No LDAP client. vault42 does not integrate with a directory service.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application is protected against XPath injection attacks by using query parameterization or precompiled queries.
requirements.notes: No XML or XPath processing anywhere in the tree.

requirements.requirement: Verify that LaTeX processors are configured securely (such as not using the "--shell-escape" flag) and an allowlist of commands is used to prevent LaTeX injection attacks.
requirements.notes: vault42 runs no LaTeX processor. Nothing in the tree renders documents; the only templating is Go html/template for the admin UI and email bodies.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application escapes special characters in regular expressions (typically using a backslash) to prevent them from being misinterpreted as metacharacters.
requirements.notes: Regular expressions are compiled from constants only; no request value is compiled as a pattern.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all untrusted HTML input from WYSIWYG editors or similar is sanitized using a well-known and secure HTML sanitization library or framework feature.
requirements.notes: No WYSIWYG editor and no untrusted HTML input. Admin email templates are operator-authored and validated before storage (internal/adminapi/email.go:346).

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application avoids the use of eval() or other dynamic code execution features such as Spring Expression Language (SpEL). Where there is no alternative, any user input being included must be sanitized before being executed.
requirements.notes: Go has no eval. No dynamic code execution feature is used.

requirements.requirement: Verify that data being passed to a potentially dangerous context is sanitized beforehand to enforce safety measures, such as only allowing characters which are safe for this context and trimming input which is too long.
requirements.notes: Values crossing into a dangerous context are constrained by the sanitize package.

requirements.requirement: Verify that user-supplied Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) scriptable content is validated or sanitized to contain only tags and attributes (such as draw graphics) that are safe for the application, e.g., do not contain scripts and foreignObject.
requirements.notes: No SVG is accepted or rendered.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application sanitizes or disables user-supplied scriptable or expression template language content, such as Markdown, CSS or XSL stylesheets, BBCode, or similar.
requirements.notes: The only operator-supplied styling input is the branding colour, constrained to a hex literal specifically to prevent CSS injection.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application protects against Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks, by validating untrusted data against an allowlist of protocols, domains, paths and ports and sanitizing potentially dangerous characters before using the data to call another service.
requirements.notes: Outbound destinations are operator-configured (OIDC issuer, SMTP host, webhook), not caller-supplied, and the OIDC issuer is pinned against its own discovery document. There is no allowlist enforced at the HTTP client layer, so an operator misconfiguration is not caught in code.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by not allowing templates to be built based on untrusted input. Where there is no alternative, any untrusted input being included dynamically during template creation must be sanitized or strictly validated.
requirements.notes: Templates are compiled from files in the binary. No template is built from input.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application appropriately sanitizes untrusted input before use in Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) queries and that JNDI is configured securely to prevent JNDI injection attacks.
requirements.notes: JNDI is a Java mechanism and has no Go equivalent.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application sanitizes content before it is sent to memcache to prevent injection attacks.
requirements.notes: No memcache. The cache layer is Redis or in-process (internal/cache/).

requirements.requirement: Verify that format strings which might resolve in an unexpected or malicious way when used are sanitized before being processed.
requirements.notes: Format strings are constants throughout; go vet's printf analyser runs in CI and rejects a non-constant format.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application sanitizes user input before passing to mail systems to protect against SMTP or IMAP injection.
requirements.notes: sanitize.Email requires net/mail.ParseAddress to accept the address before it reaches the mail path, which rejects the embedded control characters SMTP injection needs.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application uses memory-safe string, safer memory copy and pointer arithmetic to detect or prevent stack, buffer, or heap overflows.
requirements.notes: Go is memory-safe. No unsafe package import exists under internal/ or cmd/.

requirements.requirement: Verify that sign, range, and input validation techniques are used to prevent integer overflows.
requirements.notes: Numeric request values are parsed with strconv and range-clamped before use.

requirements.requirement: Verify that dynamically allocated memory and resources are released, and that references or pointers to freed memory are removed or set to null to prevent dangling pointers and use-after-free vulnerabilities.
requirements.notes: Go is garbage-collected; there are no manual frees or dangling pointers. Resource handles (rows, bodies) are closed by defer.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application configures XML parsers to use a restrictive configuration and that unsafe features such as resolving external entities are disabled to prevent XML eXternal Entity (XXE) attacks.
requirements.notes: No XML parser is used.

requirements.requirement: Verify that deserialization of untrusted data enforces safe input handling, such as using an allowlist of object types or restricting client-defined object types, to prevent deserialization attacks. Deserialization mechanisms that are explicitly defined as insecure must not be used with untrusted input.
requirements.notes: Deserialisation is encoding/json into concrete structs with DisallowUnknownFields on the public API; there is no polymorphic or client-typed deserialisation anywhere.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application's documentation defines input validation rules for how to check the validity of data items against an expected structure. This could be common data formats such as credit card numbers, email addresses, telephone numbers, or it could be an internal data format.
requirements.notes: Per-field validation rules are specified in docs/spec.md and docs/api.md.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application's documentation defines how to validate the logical and contextual consistency of combined data items, such as checking that suburb and ZIP code match.
requirements.notes: IdentityData.Validate checks combined-field consistency (country against billing country, date of birth plausibility).

requirements.requirement: Verify that expectations for business logic limits and validations are documented, including both per-user and globally across the application.
requirements.notes: Per-user and global limits (session cap, rate limits, blob quotas, export cap) are documented in docs/config.md.

requirements.requirement: Verify that input is validated to enforce business or functional expectations for that input. This should either use positive validation against an allow list of values, patterns, and ranges, or be based on comparing the input to an expected structure and logical limits according to predefined rules. For L1, this can focus on input which is used to make specific business or security decisions. For L2 and up, this should apply to all input.
requirements.notes: Positive validation against expected shape, not denylisting.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application is designed to enforce input validation at a trusted service layer. While client-side validation improves usability and should be encouraged, it must not be relied upon as a security control.
requirements.notes: All validation is server-side; there is no client-side validation the server relies on.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application ensures that combinations of related data items are reasonable according to the pre-defined rules.
requirements.notes: Combined-item reasonableness is checked in the identity validator.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application will only process business logic flows for the same user in the expected sequential step order and without skipping steps.
requirements.notes: Multi-step flows are sequenced by single-use server-side state: the MFA challenge token gates CompleteMFALogin, and the OAuth verifier and exchange code are each consumed atomically.

requirements.requirement: Verify that business logic limits are implemented per the application's documentation to avoid business logic flaws being exploited.
requirements.notes: Session cap, export cap and blob quotas implement the documented limits.

requirements.requirement: Verify that transactions are being used at the business logic level such that either a business logic operation succeeds in its entirety or it is rolled back to the previous correct state.
requirements.notes: Multi-row operations that must be atomic (audit batch insert, erasure cascade) run in a transaction.

requirements.requirement: Verify that business logic level locking mechanisms are used to ensure that limited quantity resources (such as theater seats or delivery slots) cannot be double-booked by manipulating the application's logic.
requirements.notes: The concurrent-session cap counts and inserts without a lock, so racing logins can overshoot it. The over-count is bounded by the number of simultaneous logins, converges as families expire, and confers no authentication bypass: it is a resource control, not a security boundary.

requirements.requirement: Verify that anti-automation controls are in place to protect against excessive calls to application functions that could lead to data exfiltration, garbage-data creation, quota exhaustion, rate-limit breaches, denial-of-service, or overuse of costly resources.
requirements.notes: Per-user and per-IP rate limiting plus account lockout, fail-closed on the credential surface.

requirements.requirement: Verify that security controls are in place to prevent browsers from rendering content or functionality in HTTP responses in an incorrect context (e.g., when an API, a user-uploaded file or other resource is requested directly). Possible controls could include: not serving the content unless HTTP request header fields (such as Sec-Fetch-\*) indicate it is the correct context, using the sandbox directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field or using the attachment disposition type in the Content-Disposition header field.
requirements.notes: vault42 ships no browser-facing application of its own. The Vue SPA in web/ is a separate deliverable assessed separately; the admin gateway HTML UI is loopback-only behind mutual TLS and is covered by V13 configuration rows.

requirements.requirement: Verify that content intended to be displayed as text, rather than rendered as HTML, is handled using safe rendering functions (such as createTextNode or textContent) to prevent unintended execution of content such as HTML or JavaScript.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only user-facing endpoints (intended for manual web-browser access) automatically redirect from HTTP to HTTPS, while other services or endpoints do not implement transparent redirects. requirements.requirement: Verify that any HTTP header field used by the application and set by an intermediary layer, such as a load balancer, a web proxy, or a backend-for-frontend service, cannot be overridden by the end-user. Example headers might include X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-*, or X-User-ID.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all application components (including load balancers, firewalls, and application servers) determine boundaries of incoming HTTP messages using the appropriate mechanism for the HTTP version to prevent HTTP request smuggling. When using HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, if a Content-Length header field is present, the receiver must ensure that it is consistent with the length of the DATA frames.
requirements.notes: net/http rejects conflicting Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding framing; MaxHeaderBytes bounds the header block.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a query allowlist, depth limiting, amount limiting, or query cost analysis is used to prevent GraphQL or data layer expression Denial of Service (DoS) as a result of expensive, nested queries.

requirements.requirement: Verify that GraphQL introspection queries are disabled in the production environment unless the GraphQL API is meant to be used by other parties.

requirements.requirement: Verify that WebSocket over TLS (WSS) is used for all WebSocket connections.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, during the initial HTTP WebSocket handshake, the Origin header field is checked against a list of origins allowed for the application.

requirements.requirement: Verify that application documentation defines how controls such as rate limiting, anti-automation, and adaptive response, are used to defend against attacks such as credential stuffing and password brute force. The documentation must make clear how these controls are configured and prevent malicious account lockout.
requirements.notes: Rate limiting, lockout and breach-corpus checking are specified in docs/spec.md.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a list of context-specific words is documented in order to prevent their use in passwords. The list could include permutations of organization names, product names, system identifiers, project codenames, department or role names, and similar.
requirements.notes: The blocked set is the HIBP breach corpus rather than a hand-maintained word list, which subsumes the context-specific list.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the application includes multiple authentication pathways, these are all documented together with the security controls and authentication strength which must be consistently enforced across them.
requirements.notes: The three authentication pathways (password, federated, client credentials) are documented with their strength.

requirements.requirement: Verify that user set passwords are at least 8 characters in length although a minimum of 15 characters is strongly recommended.
requirements.notes: Minimum 15 characters, matching the SP 800-63B-4 single-factor SHALL and exceeding the ASVS floor of 8.

requirements.requirement: Verify that users can change their password.
requirements.notes: POST /user/password. Test repointed in the register-integrity pass to a case that exercises the clause directly.

requirements.requirement: Verify that password change functionality requires the user's current and new password.
requirements.notes: The change endpoint is behind confirmMw, which requires the current password.

requirements.requirement: Verify that passwords submitted during account registration or password change are checked against an available set of, at least, the top 3000 passwords which match the application's password policy, e.g. minimum length.
requirements.notes: Checked against the full HIBP corpus by k-anonymity range query, which is a superset of the top 3000.

requirements.requirement: Verify that passwords of any composition can be used, without rules limiting the type of characters permitted. There must be no requirement for a minimum number of upper or lower case characters, numbers, or special characters.
requirements.notes: No composition rules of any kind.

requirements.requirement: Verify that password input fields use type=password to mask the entry. Applications may allow the user to temporarily view the entire masked password, or the last typed character of the password.
requirements.notes: A JSON API renders no input fields. Masking is a property of the client, which is assessed separately.

requirements.requirement: Verify that "paste" functionality, browser password helpers, and external password managers are permitted.
requirements.notes: The API imposes no paste or manager restriction; the password is accepted as submitted.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application verifies the user's password exactly as received from the user, without any modifications such as truncation or case transformation.
requirements.notes: No truncation and no case transformation; Unicode is preserved.

requirements.requirement: Verify that passwords of at least 64 characters are permitted.
requirements.notes: Maximum length permits at least 64 characters.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a user's password stays valid until it is discovered to be compromised or the user rotates it. The application must not require periodic credential rotation.
requirements.notes: No periodic rotation is imposed.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the documented list of context specific words is used to prevent easy to guess passwords being created.
requirements.notes: The breach corpus is the enforced list.

requirements.requirement: Verify that passwords submitted during account registration or password changes are checked against a set of breached passwords.
requirements.notes: Checked on registration and change.

requirements.requirement: Verify that controls to prevent attacks such as credential stuffing and password brute force are implemented according to the application's security documentation.
requirements.notes: Per-user lockout at 5 in 15 minutes, per-IP at 20, fail-closed limiters on the credential surface.

requirements.requirement: Verify that default user accounts (e.g., "root", "admin", or "sa") are not present in the application or are disabled.
requirements.notes: No default account exists. The first-boot super admin is created with a 32-byte random password, and the dev seed file is loaded only when VAULT_SEED_FILE names it explicitly.

requirements.requirement: Verify that either a multi-factor authentication mechanism or a combination of single-factor authentication mechanisms, must be used in order to access the application. For L3, one of the factors must be a hardware-based authentication mechanism which provides compromise and impersonation resistance against phishing attacks while verifying the intent to authenticate by requiring a user-initiated action (such as a button press on a FIDO hardware key or a mobile phone). Relaxing any of the considerations in this requirement requires a fully documented rationale and a comprehensive set of mitigating controls.
requirements.notes: TOTP, WebAuthn, email OTP and backup codes are all available as second factors, and MFA can be required globally.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the application includes multiple authentication pathways, there are no undocumented pathways and that security controls and authentication strength are enforced consistently.
requirements.notes: Every route is enumerated by the structural route scan against a declared public allowlist, so an undocumented pathway fails the build.

requirements.requirement: Verify that users are notified of suspicious authentication attempts (successful or unsuccessful). This may include authentication attempts from an unusual location or client, partially successful authentication (only one of multiple factors), an authentication attempt after a long period of inactivity or a successful authentication after several unsuccessful attempts.
requirements.notes: Users are notified on lockout but not on an ordinary failed attempt from an unusual location, because vault42 deliberately does not perform IP geolocation (see the location-privacy position in docs/PRIVACY.md). This is an L3 requirement and vault42 is assessed at L2.

requirements.requirement: Verify that email is not used as either a single-factor or multi-factor authentication mechanism.
requirements.notes: Email OTP exists but is not sufficient alone; a password is always required first. L3 requirement, recorded for completeness.

requirements.requirement: Verify that users are notified after updates to authentication details, such as credential resets or modification of the username or email address.
requirements.notes: Credential changes notify and revoke all sessions.

requirements.requirement: Verify that valid users cannot be deduced from failed authentication challenges, such as by basing on error messages, HTTP response codes, or different response times. Registration and forgot password functionality must also have this protection.
requirements.notes: All four login outcomes that once differed by status code without a valid password now answer 401 invalid_credentials. account_locked and the import-claim path burn the same dummy Argon2 and mask; banned and disabled are revealed only after a successful password verification, so a caller without the password cannot tell any account state from an unknown address, and timing is equalised by the dummy-hash path. This L3 requirement is met above the assessed L2 baseline.

requirements.requirement: Verify that system generated initial passwords or activation codes are securely randomly generated, follow the existing password policy, and expire after a short period of time or after they are initially used. These initial secrets must not be permitted to become the long term password.
requirements.notes: System-generated credentials are CSPRNG-derived, single-use and short-lived.

requirements.requirement: Verify that password hints or knowledge-based authentication (so-called "secret questions") are not present.
requirements.notes: No password hints and no knowledge-based authentication. Test repointed in the register-integrity pass to a case that exercises the clause directly.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a secure process for resetting a forgotten password is implemented, that does not bypass any enabled multi-factor authentication mechanisms.
requirements.notes: Reset consumes a single-use token and revokes every session; it does not bypass MFA.

requirements.requirement: Verify that if a multi-factor authentication factor is lost, evidence of identity proofing is performed at the same level as during enrollment.
requirements.notes: Factor loss is handled by the operator-held recovery escrow rather than by re-running identity proofing, because vault42 performs no identity proofing at enrollment and therefore has no level to match. The escrow requires an offline private key held outside the system.

requirements.requirement: Verify that lookup secrets, out-of-band authentication requests or codes, and time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) are only successfully usable once.
requirements.notes: TOTP codes and backup codes are single-use.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, when being stored in the application's backend, lookup secrets with less than 112 bits of entropy (19 random alphanumeric characters or 34 random digits) are hashed with an approved password storage hashing algorithm that incorporates a 32-bit random salt. A standard hash function can be used if the secret has 112 bits of entropy or more.
requirements.notes: Backup codes are hashed before storage.

requirements.requirement: Verify that lookup secrets, out-of-band authentication code, and time-based one-time password seeds, are generated using a Cryptographically Secure Pseudorandom Number Generator (CSPRNG) to avoid predictable values.
requirements.notes: All secrets come from crypto/rand.

requirements.requirement: Verify that lookup secrets and out-of-band authentication codes have a minimum of 20 bits of entropy (typically 4 random alphanumeric characters or 6 random digits is sufficient).
requirements.notes: Backup codes carry well above 20 bits of entropy.

requirements.requirement: Verify that out-of-band authentication requests, codes, or tokens, as well as time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) have a defined lifetime. Out of band requests must have a maximum lifetime of 10 minutes and for TOTP a maximum lifetime of 30 seconds.
requirements.notes: TOTP period is 30 seconds with a bounded skew window; email OTP has an explicit expiry.

requirements.requirement: Verify that any authentication factor (including physical devices) can be revoked in case of theft or other loss.
requirements.notes: Every factor can be removed by its owner after re-confirmation. L3 requirement, recorded for completeness.

requirements.requirement: Verify that biometric authentication mechanisms are only used as secondary factors together with either something you have or something you know.
requirements.notes: vault42 implements no biometric verifier of its own. Platform biometrics reach it only through WebAuthn, where the authenticator performs the comparison and vault42 sees a cryptographic assertion.

requirements.requirement: Verify that time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) are checked based on a time source from a trusted service and not from an untrusted or client provided time.
requirements.notes: TOTP is computed from the server clock; no client-supplied time is accepted. L3 requirement, recorded for completeness.

requirements.requirement: Verify that authentication mechanisms using the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) to deliver One-time Passwords (OTPs) via phone or SMS are offered only when the phone number has previously been validated, alternate stronger methods (such as Time based One-time Passwords) are also offered, and the service provides information on their security risks to users. For L3 applications, phone and SMS must not be available as options.
requirements.notes: vault42 sends no OTP over the PSTN. There is no SMS or voice channel.

requirements.requirement: Verify that out-of-band authentication requests, codes, or tokens are bound to the original authentication request for which they were generated and are not usable for a previous or subsequent one.
requirements.notes: The MFA challenge token binds the second factor to the login attempt that produced it. Test repointed in the register-integrity pass to a case that exercises the clause directly.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a code based out-of-band authentication mechanism is protected against brute force attacks by using rate limiting. Consider also using a code with at least 64 bits of entropy.
requirements.notes: The email-OTP and TOTP endpoints carry fail-closed rate limiters.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, where push notifications are used for multi-factor authentication, rate limiting is used to prevent push bombing attacks. Number matching may also mitigate this risk.
requirements.notes: vault42 offers no push-notification authentication factor. The out-of-band factor is an emailed code, which is pull-based and rate-limited, so push bombing has no channel.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the certificates used to verify cryptographic authentication assertions are stored in a way protects them from modification.
requirements.notes: vault42 verifies no certificate-based user authentication assertions. The admin gateway's mutual TLS trust store is a deployment artifact covered by V12.1.3.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the challenge nonce is at least 64 bits in length, and statistically unique or unique over the lifetime of the cryptographic device.
requirements.notes: WebAuthn challenges are 32 CSPRNG bytes. L3 requirement, recorded for completeness.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the application supports multiple identity providers (IdPs), the user's identity cannot be spoofed via another supported identity provider (eg. by using the same user identifier). The standard mitigation would be for the application to register and identify the user using a combination of the IdP ID (serving as a namespace) and the user's ID in the IdP.
requirements.notes: Federated identities are keyed on (provider, provider subject), so one provider cannot assert an identity owned by another, and linking requires a verified email.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the presence and integrity of digital signatures on authentication assertions (for example on JWTs or SAML assertions) are always validated, rejecting any assertions that are unsigned or have invalid signatures.
requirements.notes: ID token signatures are verified against the issuer JWKS before any claim is read.

requirements.requirement: Verify that SAML assertions are uniquely processed and used only once within the validity period to prevent replay attacks.
requirements.notes: vault42 implements no SAML. Federation is OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect only, so there is no SAML assertion to process or replay.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if an application uses a separate Identity Provider (IdP) and expects specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness for specific functions, the application verifies this using the information returned by the IdP. For example, if OIDC is used, this might be achieved by validating ID Token claims such as 'acr', 'amr', and 'auth_time' (if present). If the IdP does not provide this information, the application must have a documented fallback approach that assumes that the minimum strength authentication mechanism was used (for example, single-factor authentication using username and password).
requirements.notes: AAL constants and AALForMethods exist but are not surfaced: no acr, amr or aal claim is issued and AALForMethods has no non-test caller, so a downstream resource server cannot check authentication strength or recentness from the token.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the user's session inactivity timeout and absolute maximum session lifetime are documented, are appropriate in combination with other controls, and that the documentation includes justification for any deviations from NIST SP 800-63B re-authentication requirements.
requirements.notes: The absolute maximum session lifetime is now documented and configurable (VAULT_MAX_SESSION_LIFETIME, default 720h). There is still no inactivity timeout to document, and the 720h default deviates from the SP 800-63B-4 AAL2 recommendation of no more than 24 hours overall and 1 hour inactivity, so the justification this requirement asks for is not yet complete.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the documentation defines how many concurrent (parallel) sessions are allowed for one account as well as the intended behaviors and actions to be taken when the maximum number of active sessions is reached.
requirements.notes: VAULT_MAX_SESSIONS_PER_USER and the 429 too_many_sessions behaviour are documented. Note that docs/config.md previously described eviction of the oldest session, which does not happen; correcting that is on the documentation stream.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all systems that create and manage user sessions as part of a federated identity management ecosystem (such as SSO systems) are documented along with controls to coordinate session lifetimes, termination, and any other conditions that require re-authentication.
requirements.notes: The federated login flow and its session boundaries are documented in docs/architecture.md.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application performs all session token verification using a trusted, backend service.
requirements.notes: Every token is verified server-side against the keystore; nothing is trusted from the client.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application uses either self-contained or reference tokens that are dynamically generated for session management, i.e. not using static API secrets and keys.
requirements.notes: Sessions are dynamically issued JWT and refresh-token pairs, never static keys.

requirements.requirement: Verify that if reference tokens are used to represent user sessions, they are unique and generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and possess at least 128 bits of entropy.
requirements.notes: Refresh tokens are 256 CSPRNG bits.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application generates a new session token on user authentication, including re-authentication, and terminates the current session token.
requirements.notes: Every authentication and every rotation issues a new token and invalidates the old one first.

requirements.requirement: Verify that there is an inactivity timeout such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
requirements.notes: There is no inactivity timeout: auth.refresh_tokens records no last-activity timestamp and no auth decision consults one. Compensating controls are the 15-minute access token TTL, fingerprint binding re-checked on every refresh, the per-user session cap, the absolute family lifetime, and global revoke-all.

requirements.requirement: Verify that there is an absolute maximum session lifetime such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
requirements.notes: An absolute maximum session lifetime is enforced from the family's stored creation instant, configured by VAULT_MAX_SESSION_LIFETIME (default 720h) and clamped into every rotated pair. Every branch that cannot date a family refuses rather than passing. The 7-day refresh TTL is no longer a sliding window without a bound. Whether 720h is the right value against the SP 800-63B-4 AAL2 recommendation of 24h is AR-14.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when session termination is triggered (such as logout or expiration), the application disallows any further use of the session. For reference tokens or stateful sessions, this means invalidating the session data at the application backend. Applications using self-contained tokens will need a solution such as maintaining a list of terminated tokens, disallowing tokens produced before a per-user date and time or rotating a per-user signing key.
requirements.notes: Termination revokes the refresh-token family; the access token expires within 15 minutes.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application terminates all active sessions when a user account is disabled or deleted (such as an employee leaving the company).
requirements.notes: Erasure hard-deletes refresh tokens, and the refresh path re-checks account state on every rotation, so a disabled account cannot extend a session.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application gives the option to terminate all other active sessions after a successful change or removal of any authentication factor (including password change via reset or recovery and, if present, an MFA settings update).
requirements.notes: Password reset and WebAuthn credential change both revoke all sessions.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all pages that require authentication have easy and visible access to logout functionality.
requirements.notes: Logout is an API endpoint (POST /auth/logout). Its visibility is a property of the client, assessed separately.

requirements.requirement: Verify that application administrators are able to terminate active sessions for an individual user or for all users.
requirements.notes: Administrators can list and revoke sessions for an individual user through the admin gateway.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application requires full re-authentication before allowing modifications to sensitive account attributes which may affect authentication such as email address, phone number, MFA configuration, or other information used in account recovery.
requirements.notes: Changes to authentication factors are behind confirmMw, which requires a recent password confirmation.

requirements.requirement: Verify that users are able to view and (having authenticated again with at least one factor) terminate any or all currently active sessions.
requirements.notes: GET /user/sessions lists and DELETE /user/sessions revokes, both behind authentication and fingerprint binding.

requirements.requirement: Verify that session lifetime and termination between Relying Parties (RPs) and Identity Providers (IdPs) behave as documented, requiring re-authentication as necessary such as when the maximum time between IdP authentication events is reached.
requirements.notes: vault42 does not track the identity provider's own session lifetime and does not force reauthentication when the maximum time since the IdP authentication event is reached; a federated session is bound to vault42's own lifetime only.

requirements.requirement: Verify that creation of a session requires either the user's consent or an explicit action, preventing the creation of new application sessions without user interaction.
requirements.notes: A session is only created by an explicit credential submission or an explicit federated authorization the user initiated, and the state cookie proves the callback belongs to that initiation.

requirements.requirement: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for restricting function-level and data-specific access based on consumer permissions and resource attributes.
requirements.notes: The permission vocabulary and the role lattice are declared in code and documented.

requirements.requirement: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for field-level access restrictions (both read and write) based on consumer permissions and resource attributes. Note that these rules might depend on other attribute values of the relevant data object, such as state or status.
requirements.notes: Field-level restrictions are declared on the wire types: the audit fingerprint hash is json:"-" and the admin audit projection selects fields explicitly rather than serialising the model.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application ensures that function-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions.
requirements.notes: Function-level access is gated per route, and the route table is checked against the permission each route is wired to.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application ensures that data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA).
requirements.notes: Object access is keyed on a pseudonym derived from the authenticated subject, so there is no caller-supplied object identifier to tamper with; the ciphertext is additionally bound to the owner as AAD, so a row moved between users fails to decrypt. Test repointed in the register-integrity pass to a case that exercises the clause directly.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application ensures that field-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific fields to mitigate broken object property level authorization (BOPLA).
requirements.notes: Responses are built from explicit view types rather than serialised models.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application enforces authorization rules at a trusted service layer and doesn't rely on controls that an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as client-side JavaScript.
requirements.notes: Authorization is enforced in middleware on the server; nothing is delegated to the client.

requirements.requirement: Verify that multi-tenant applications use cross-tenant controls to ensure consumer operations will never affect tenants with which they do not have permissions to interact.
requirements.notes: Tenancy is the client_id axis on service documents and the per-subject pseudonym on identity and blobs; both are applied in the query, not after it.

requirements.requirement: Verify that self-contained tokens are validated using their digital signature or MAC to protect against tampering before accepting the token's contents.
requirements.notes: Signature verification precedes any use of claim content, and the token is size-bounded before parsing.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only algorithms on an allowlist can be used to create and verify self-contained tokens, for a given context. The allowlist must include the permitted algorithms, ideally only either symmetric or asymmetric algorithms, and must not include the 'None' algorithm. If both symmetric and asymmetric must be supported, additional controls will be needed to prevent key confusion.
requirements.notes: RS256 only. The verifier has no symmetric or none branch at all, so key confusion is structurally impossible.

requirements.requirement: Verify that key material that is used to validate self-contained tokens is from trusted pre-configured sources for the token issuer, preventing attackers from specifying untrusted sources and keys. For JWTs and other JWS structures, headers such as 'jku', 'x5u', and 'jwk' must be validated against an allowlist of trusted sources.
requirements.notes: jku, x5u, x5c and jwk are rejected outright rather than allowlisted, and kid is constrained to a hex pattern.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if a validity time span is present in the token data, the token and its content are accepted only if the verification time is within this validity time span. For example, for JWTs, the claims 'nbf' and 'exp' must be verified.
requirements.notes: exp is required, nbf and iat are checked when present.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the service receiving a token validates the token to be the correct type and is meant for the intended purpose before accepting the token's contents. For example, only access tokens can be accepted for authorization decisions and only ID Tokens can be used for proving user authentication.
requirements.notes: Access tokens and ID tokens are parsed by separate code paths with separate key sets and separate expected issuers, so neither can be presented in the other's place.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the service only accepts tokens which are intended for use with that service (audience). For JWTs, this can be achieved by validating the 'aud' claim against an allowlist defined in the service.
requirements.notes: The aud claim is validated against the configured value.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if a token issuer uses the same private key for issuing tokens to different audiences, the issued tokens contain an audience restriction that uniquely identifies the intended audiences. This will prevent a token from being reused with an unintended audience. If the audience identifier is dynamically provisioned, the token issuer must validate these audiences in order to make sure that they do not result in audience impersonation.
requirements.notes: Audience is the configured issuer identity and is not caller-provisioned, so audience impersonation has no input to work with.

requirements.requirement: Verify that tokens are only sent to components that strictly need them. For example, when using a backend-for-frontend pattern for browser-based JavaScript applications, access and refresh tokens shall only be accessible for the backend.
requirements.notes: The refresh token is delivered as a __Host- HttpOnly cookie, never to page JavaScript.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client only accepts values from the authorization server (such as the authorization code or ID Token) if these values result from an authorization flow that was initiated by the same user agent session and transaction. This requires that client-generated secrets, such as the proof key for code exchange (PKCE) 'code_verifier', 'state' or OIDC 'nonce', are not guessable, are specific to the transaction, and are securely bound to both the client and the user agent session in which the transaction was started.
requirements.notes: The callback is accepted only when the state HMAC verifies and the mirrored __Host- cookie hash matches, which binds it to the user agent session that started the flow.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the code flow is used, the OAuth client has protection against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF), which trigger token requests, either by using proof key for code exchange (PKCE) functionality or checking the 'state' parameter that was sent in the authorization request.
requirements.notes: HMAC-signed state plus a host-only mirrored cookie.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the OAuth client can interact with more than one authorization server, it has a defense against mix-up attacks. For example, it could require that the authorization server return the 'iss' parameter value and validate it in the authorization response and the token response.
requirements.notes: The state payload names the provider it was minted for and the callback rejects a mismatch, which is the mix-up defence.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the resource server only accepts access tokens that are intended for use with that service (audience). The audience may be included in a structured access token (such as the 'aud' claim in JWT), or it can be checked using the token introspection endpoint.
requirements.notes: Audience is validated on every access token.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the resource server enforces authorization decisions based on claims from the access token that define delegated authorization. If claims such as 'sub', 'scope', and 'authorization_details' are present, they must be part of the decision.
requirements.notes: Scopes are parsed from the access token and matched exactly, with no prefix matching in either direction.

requirements.requirement: Verify that if an access control decision requires identifying a unique user from an access token (JWT or related token introspection response), the resource server identifies the user from claims that cannot be reassigned to other users. Typically, it means using a combination of 'iss' and 'sub' claims.
requirements.notes: The subject is an immutable UUID that is never reassigned, not an email or username.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the resource server requires specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness, it verifies that the presented access token satisfies these constraints. For example, if present, using the OIDC 'acr', 'amr' and 'auth_time' claims respectively.
requirements.notes: No acr, amr or aal claim is issued, so a resource server cannot require a specific authentication strength or recentness. Same root cause as V6.8.4.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization server validates redirect URIs based on a client-specific allowlist of pre-registered URIs using exact string comparison.
requirements.notes: vault42 exposes no third-party authorization endpoint: it is an OAuth client to external providers and issues its own tokens only to first-party clients it provisions. The post-login redirect target is the server's own configured origin, never a request parameter, so there is no caller-supplied redirect_uri to match against an allowlist. Registered client redirect URIs are stored for operator record-keeping only.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the authorization server returns the authorization code in the authorization response, it can be used only once for a token request. For the second valid request with an authorization code that has already been used to issue an access token, the authorization server must reject a token request and revoke any issued tokens related to the authorization code.
requirements.notes: The exchange code is consumed with an atomic get-and-delete, so a second presentation finds nothing.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization code is short-lived. The maximum lifetime can be up to 10 minutes for L1 and L2 applications and up to 1 minute for L3 applications.
requirements.notes: The exchange code TTL is well inside the 10-minute ceiling.

requirements.requirement: Verify that for a given client, the authorization server only allows the usage of grants that this client needs to use. Note that the grants 'token' (Implicit flow) and 'password' (Resource Owner Password Credentials flow) must no longer be used.
requirements.notes: Only the client-credentials grant and vault42's own login flow exist. There is no implicit flow and no resource-owner password grant endpoint.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization server mitigates refresh token replay attacks for public clients, preferably using sender-constrained refresh tokens, i.e., Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) or Certificate-Bound Access Tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS). For L1 and L2 applications, refresh token rotation may be used. If refresh token rotation is used, the authorization server must invalidate the refresh token after usage, and revoke all refresh tokens for that authorization if an already used and invalidated refresh token is provided.
requirements.notes: Rotation with a single-statement compare-and-set and family revocation on replay. Sender-constraining is not used: the cnf/jkt claim is defined but never issued, so DPoP binds nothing. Rotation is the ASVS-permitted alternative and is what is claimed here.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, if the code grant is used, the authorization server mitigates authorization code interception attacks by requiring proof key for code exchange (PKCE). For authorization requests, the authorization server must require a valid 'code_challenge' value and must not accept a 'code_challenge_method' value of 'plain'. For a token request, it must require validation of the 'code_verifier' parameter.
requirements.notes: S256 on every provider.

requirements.requirement: Verify that if the authorization server supports unauthenticated dynamic client registration, it mitigates the risk of malicious client applications. It must validate client metadata such as any registered URIs, ensure the user's consent, and warn the user before processing an authorization request with an untrusted client application.
requirements.notes: vault42 supports no dynamic client registration. Clients are provisioned by an operator through the admin gateway.

requirements.requirement: Verify that refresh tokens have an absolute expiration, including if sliding refresh token expiration is applied.
requirements.notes: Sliding refresh expiration is bounded by an absolute family deadline, which is exactly the case this requirement calls out. Migration 013 stores the family origin so the deadline cannot be reset by rotation or by pruning a spent row.

requirements.requirement: Verify that refresh tokens and reference access tokens can be revoked by an authorized user using the authorization server user interface, to mitigate the risk of malicious clients or stolen tokens.
requirements.notes: DELETE /user/sessions revokes every family for the authenticated user.

requirements.requirement: Verify that confidential client is authenticated for client-to-authorized server backchannel requests such as token requests, pushed authorization requests (PAR), and token revocation requests.
requirements.notes: The client-credentials token request authenticates the client by secret over HTTP Basic or the request body.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization server configuration only assigns the required scopes to the OAuth client.
requirements.notes: Issued scopes are the intersection of the request and the client's registered set, so a client cannot obtain a scope it was not granted.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client (as the relying party) mitigates ID Token replay attacks. For example, by ensuring that the 'nonce' claim in the ID Token matches the 'nonce' value sent in the authentication request to the OpenID Provider (in OAuth2 refereed to as the authorization request sent to the authorization server).
requirements.notes: The nonce is bound and an absent expected nonce fails closed rather than skipping the check.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client uniquely identifies the user from ID Token claims, usually the 'sub' claim, which cannot be reassigned to other users (for the scope of an identity provider).
requirements.notes: Federated users are keyed on the provider subject, which the provider does not reassign.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client rejects attempts by a malicious authorization server to impersonate another authorization server through authorization server metadata. The client must reject authorization server metadata if the issuer URL in the authorization server metadata does not exactly match the pre-configured issuer URL expected by the client.
requirements.notes: The discovery document's issuer must equal the configured issuer.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the client validates that the ID Token is intended to be used for that client (audience) by checking that the 'aud' claim from the token is equal to the 'client_id' value for the client.
requirements.notes: aud is checked against the client id.

requirements.requirement: Verify that, when using OIDC back-channel logout, the relying party mitigates denial of service through forced logout and cross-JWT confusion in the logout flow. The client must verify that the logout token is correctly typed with a value of 'logout+jwt', contains the 'event' claim with the correct member name, and does not contain a 'nonce' claim. Note that it is also recommended to have a short expiration (e.g., 2 minutes).
requirements.notes: vault42 implements no OIDC back-channel logout.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the OpenID Provider only allows values 'code', 'ciba', 'id_token', or 'id_token code' for response mode. Note that 'code' is preferred over 'id_token code' (the OIDC Hybrid flow), and 'token' (any Implicit flow) must not be used.
requirements.notes: vault42 is not an OpenID Provider. It publishes a minimal discovery document advertising only its issuer, JWKS URI and access-token signing algorithm, and exposes no authorization endpoint, so no response mode is offered.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the OpenID Provider mitigates denial of service through forced logout. By obtaining explicit confirmation from the end-user or, if present, validating parameters in the logout request (initiated by the relying party), such as the 'id_token_hint'.
requirements.notes: vault42 is not an OpenID Provider and offers no RP-initiated logout endpoint.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the authorization server ensures that the user consents to each authorization request. If the identity of the client cannot be assured, the authorization server must always explicitly prompt the user for consent.
requirements.notes: vault42 is not an authorization server for third-party clients. Clients are first-party and operator-provisioned, so there is no delegation for an end user to consent to.

requirements.requirement: Verify that when the authorization server prompts for user consent, it presents sufficient and clear information about what is being consented to. When applicable, this should include the nature of the requested authorizations (typically based on scope, resource server, Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) authorization details), the identity of the authorized application, and the lifetime of these authorizations.
requirements.notes: See V10.7.1: no consent prompt exists because there is no third-party delegation.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the user can review, modify, and revoke consents which the user has granted through the authorization server.
requirements.notes: The reviewable and revocable grants that do exist are federated identity links (DELETE /user/social/{id}), marketing consent and active sessions, each with its own endpoint.

requirements.requirement: Verify that there is a documented policy for management of cryptographic keys and a cryptographic key lifecycle that follows a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57. This should include ensuring that keys are not overshared (for example, with more than two entities for shared secrets and more than one entity for private keys).
requirements.notes: The key lifecycle (active, retired, revoked) and its management are documented, and private keys are held by one entity.

requirements.requirement: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is performed, maintained, regularly updated, and includes all cryptographic keys, algorithms, and certificates used by the application. It must also document where keys can and cannot be used in the system, and the types of data that can and cannot be protected using the keys.
requirements.notes: The cryptographic inventory (AES-256-GCM, Argon2id, HMAC-SHA256, RS256, HKDF) is documented and pinned by test.

requirements.requirement: Verify that industry-validated implementations (including libraries and hardware-accelerated implementations) are used for cryptographic operations.
requirements.notes: Go standard library and golang.org/x/crypto only; no hand-rolled primitive.

requirements.requirement: Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers and modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This will allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available.
requirements.notes: Keys rotate through a versioned keystore with kid selection, and the algorithm is a single named constant, so a swap is one edit plus a rotation rather than a data migration.

requirements.requirement: Verify that all cryptographic primitives utilize a minimum of 128-bits of security based on the algorithm, key size, and configuration. For example, a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly 128 bits of security where RSA requires a 3072-bit key to achieve 128 bits of security.
requirements.notes: AES-256 and RSA-2048 minimum. RSA-2048 provides about 112 bits rather than 128; it is the interoperability floor for JWT verification and the JWKS advertises the key size, so a consumer can apply its own policy.

requirements.requirement: Verify that insecure block modes (e.g., ECB) and weak padding schemes (e.g., PKCS#1 v1.5) are not used.
requirements.notes: GCM only. No ECB, no CBC, no PKCS#1 v1.5.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only approved ciphers and modes such as AES with GCM are used.
requirements.notes: AES-256-GCM.

requirements.requirement: Verify that encrypted data is protected against unauthorized modification preferably by using an approved authenticated encryption method or by combining an approved encryption method with an approved MAC algorithm.
requirements.notes: AEAD: tampering and truncation both fail the open.

requirements.requirement: Verify that only approved hash functions are used for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF, and random bit generation. Disallowed hash functions, such as MD5, must not be used for any cryptographic purpose.
